title: Private deployments: VPC & On-Prem deployment reference and Day-2 ops guide
author: Samantha Ortiz
content:
Overview

This page is the canonical reference for deploying Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) in production, packaging options, and Day-2 operational procedures including upgrade and rollback playbooks. It is intended for platform engineers, customer on-prem engineering teams, and Solutions Engineering during customer onboarding. Use this guide together with the runbooks and architecture pages linked in Related pages.

Scope and audience

- Scope: Deployment topologies for VPC-managed and fully on-prem (air-gapped) installs, packaging formats, pre-deployment customer requirements, step-by-step installation checklist, Day-2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling), and safe upgrade/rollback procedures.
- Audience: Platform engineers, field SREs, customer infra engineers, SEs.

Top-level design principles

1. Security-first: least privilege network flows, KMS/HSM for keys, and audit logging enabled by default.
2. Predictable performance: explicit hardware and network requirements per reference architecture.
3. Observable and reversible: upgrades are staged with health-checks and automatic rollback triggers.

Reference architectures (summary)

1) VPC-hosted (customer VPC, Redwood control plane optional)
- Typical topology: customer VPC with private subnets for inference nodes, NAT/egress, and a managed control plane endpoint (or private connectivity to Redwood control plane).
- Key components: compute subnets, model artifact store (S3-compatible), internal LB (ALB/NLB), bastion/jump host for maintenance, KMS integration (customer-managed key recommended).
- When to use: customers that require network isolation but allow egress for control plane connectivity.

2) Transit-gateway / hub-and-spoke (multi-AZ enterprise)
- Topology: Transit gateway connects multiple VPCs (platform, workloads, data), central NAT and shared services VPC for artifact storage and logging.
- Advantages: centralized security controls, shared logging, and simplified auditing.

3) Fully on-prem / air-gapped
- Topology: customer-managed datacenter, private model artifact registry, internal-only control plane and telemetry (optionally buffered to an air-gap courier).
- Packaging: OVA/VM images for closed environments or container images with Helm/OCI bundles.
- When to use: regulated workloads or customers that disallow any external connectivity.

Hardware and sizing guidance (table)

| Workload | Minimum GPU | Minimum RAM (per node) | Typical cluster size | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Small dev/test | 1 x A10 / A2 | 64 GB | 1-2 nodes | Not for production SLOs |
| Production latency (per model) | 4 x A100-40GB | 512 GB | 3-10 nodes | Use autoscaling for burst capacity |
| High-throughput batching | 8 x A100-80GB | 1 TB | 6-20 nodes | Requires high PCIe / NVLink throughput |

Pre-deployment customer requirements checklist

Network and security
- CIDR allocation for control plane, data plane, and management subnets.
- Private DNS and split-horizon details for internal routing.
- Firewall/NACL rules: allow internal ports 22 (bastion), 8200 (control plane API, example), 9090 (metrics), 443 for optional egress to artifact stores.
- VPC endpoints (S3, ECR) or local object store details.
- KMS/HSM details and key ARNs.

Identity and access
- Service account names and minimal IAM policies required.
- PKI / client cert process for mutual TLS if required.

Storage and artifact registry
- S3-compatible endpoint + credentials or NFS/Ceph details for on-prem.
- Artifact retention policy and expected model sizes.

Compliance and auditing
- Required audit log retention period (days), syslog/ELK host(s).
- Data residency constraints and allowed egress destinations.

Operational requirements
- Backup window and RPO/RTO targets, on-call rotation, escalation contacts.
- Approval for rolling reboot windows and capacity scaling policies.

Preflight checks (commands)

Run these before starting install: 
1. Network reachability: curl -f https://control-plane.redwood.example/status or test local endpoints.
2. Disk and kernel: df -h; uname -a; verify kernel >= 5.10 for required drivers.
3. GPU drivers: nvidia-smi (expected driver >= 525.xx), container runtime (containerd or docker) running.
4. Artifact store: aws s3 ls s3://redwood-models --endpoint-url <CUSTOMER_ENDPOINT>

Deployment procedure (high-level)

1) Bootstrap management plane
- Apply control-plane manifest or run the install script: 
  - Example (Helm): helm repo add redwood https://packages.redwood.example/charts && helm install redwood-control redwood/control-plane -f values.yaml
- Verify control plane health: curl -fsS http://<control-plane>/healthz  (expect 200)

2) Provision compute nodes and agents
- Use our packaging (container/Helm for k8s) or OVA for air-gapped deployments.
- Register nodes with control plane: redwood-agent enroll --token <TOKEN> --node-group inference-prod

3) Model artifact onboarding
- Upload model tarballs to artifact store and register model in control plane: 
  - redwoodctl model register --name llama-3b --uri s3://bucket/models/llama-3b.tar.gz --quantized false

4) Networking, KMS, and secrets
- Configure secrets store connector (HashiCorp Vault / KMS) and test key wrapping/unwrapping.

5) Observability and logging
- Install Prometheus node-exporter, configure metrics endpoint scraping (/metrics).
- Ensure logs flow to customer ELK or central logging via Fluentd/Vector.

6) Smoke tests and SLA validation
- Run perf harness for representative prompt sets (see prompt-sets-and-benchmarks). Validate p50/p95 latency and throughput.

Day-2 operations

Monitoring and alerting
- Essential alerts: control-plane-unavailable, agent-heartbeat-missing (>5m), GPU-memory-pressure (>90%), model-loading-errors.
- SLOs to track: inference latency (p50/p95), token throughput, error rate (5xx), model load time.

Backups and DR
- Control plane DB (encrypted) snapshot daily. Retention policy 30 days by default.
- Model artifacts should be versioned and replicated outside cluster.
- Restore drill: documented in the runbook; perform quarterly DR tests.

Scaling and capacity management
- Horizontal autoscaling: configure cluster autoscaler to add nodes when pending pods > N for 10 minutes.
- Burst capacity: maintain a warm pool of spare GPUs for predicted traffic spikes.

Routine maintenance
- Patch schedule: minor OS patches monthly; GPU driver upgrades quarterly.
- Reboot windows: apply rolling reboots with maxUnavailable=1 to maintain capacity.

Upgrade procedure (safe path)

Principles:
- Use incremental staged upgrades (canary -> partial rollout -> full).
- Automated health checks gating progress; failures trigger automated rollback.

Steps:
1. Pre-upgrade: run upgrade-readiness checks (preflight), snapshot control-plane DB, and ensure model artifacts have immutable tags.
2. Canary: upgrade 1 control-plane instance and 1 node in an isolated node group. Run smoke tests and compare metrics for 30 minutes.
3. Partial rollout: 10-30% of nodes. Monitor errors and latency for 2 hours.
4. Full rollout: remaining nodes in rolling fashion, respecting maxUnavailable.
5. Post-upgrade validation: run end-to-end evals tying to expected quality metrics and validate billing/usage datapoints.

Automatic rollback triggers:
- Control plane health check fail (HTTP 200 -> non-200) for > 5 minutes.
- p95 latency increase > 35% vs baseline for 15 minutes.
- Error rate 5xx > 2% for 10 minutes.

Rollback procedure (manual intervention)

1. Stop rollout and mark the release as halted in the control plane.
2. Revert control-plane manifest / Helm release to previous version: helm rollback redwood-control <REVISION>
3. For agents/nodes, cordon affected nodes and redeploy previous agent image: kubectl set image daemonset/redwood-agent redwood-agent=redwood/agent:<previous-tag>
4. Validate health and gradually uncordon nodes.
5. Postmortem and customer notification: follow the incident review template and notify stakeholders per Escalation Playbook.

Common troubleshooting scenarios

- Node failing to register: check agent logs (/var/log/redwood-agent.log), validate enrollment token and control plane reachability.
- Model load failures: verify artifact checksum, available GPU memory, and model config (vocab/tokenizer mismatches).
- Performance regressions: compare p50/p95 vs baseline; check NVLink/PCIe errors and kernel GPU driver versions.

Operational ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (on-call rota: eng-pd-oncall@redwood.com).
- Escalation: oncall -> platform-sre -> CTO (see escalation-playbook).

Appendix: sample values.yaml (Helm)

# Minimum example values for production deployment
controlPlane:
  replicas: 3
  image: "redwood/control-plane:1.4.0"
api:
  bindAddress: "0.0.0.0"
  port: 8200
agent:
  image: "redwood/agent:1.4.0"
  nodeSelector: "gpu=true"
modelStore:
  type: s3
  endpoint: "https://s3.example-customer.internal"
  bucket: "redwood-models"
kms:
  provider: aws-kms
  keyArn: "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/abcd-ef01"
observability:
  prometheus:
    enabled: true
    scrape_interval: 15s
logging:
  driver: fluentd
